subject: iceCreamCart
reasoning:
I'm planning out an ice cream cart design using blocky stylized primitives—wheels, a striped canopy, a freezer box with a serving window, cone-shaped scoops on a dome, and a sign—using bold colors and no joints since it's not a creature.

Working out dimensions and part placement...

With wheel radius 0.14, the body sits from y=0.3 to 1.0. I'm adding a front serving counter box, a dark inset window opening, and a striped awning using the stripes paint function with bands running along the x-axis to create vertical candy-stripe bands across the canopy.

For the awning I'm tilting it forward using an X-axis rotation (around 12 degrees) so the front edge dips down, positioned above the window with corner posts built from rod primitives. I'm also considering topping the cart with a decorative ice cream cone sign using a lathe profile.

Working out the scoop geometry...

Now I'm thinking about placement: stacking pink, mint, chocolate, and vanilla scoops on a cone as a decorative sign on top of the cart's roof, maybe mounted on a pole above the roofline around height 1.9.

I'm working out the cone dimensions, scoop sizes and positions stacked with slight overlap, plus a small red cherry sphere on top, before moving on to the wheels—cylinders rotated to sit as tires with dark rubber and cream hubs on either side of the cart.

I'm now sketching the undercarriage as a dark flat box sitting above the wheels, then defining the main cart body as a box with a pastel mint color, picking out a palette of cream, red, pink, and brown accents for the trim.

I'm adding a cream trim band near the top and a red trim strip at the bottom, then building out a protruding front counter box and a dark glass window panel that I want to feel lit up with a warm vanilla glow.

Since the body is a solid box, I realize I can't truly carve a window into it, so I'm layering a lit panel decal on the front face instead, framed by thin cream boxes, and adding a few small colorful tub cylinders sitting on the counter top for extra detail.

Then I'm working out a tilted striped awning above the window, positioning its hinge and depth so it overhangs the front without crashing into the counter, and sketching in diagonal support rods running from the counter corners up to the awning's front edge to hold it up visually.

I decide to skip the fiddly scalloped valance edge along the awning (tried spheres and rotated cylinder discs but they're unreliable) and just rely on the painted stripes to read as decoration instead. Then I add a flat canopy roof box above the body, supported by corner posts rising from the body top to the roof, with cream trim, and start planning a large sign/cone element sitting on top of the canopy.

I work out the geometry for a stacked ice-cream cone sign: a lathe-shaped cone with its tip pointing down and widening toward the top, topped by three overlapping scoop spheres of decreasing radius and finally a cherry, aiming for a total cart height of about 2.5 meters, which feels close enough to a real cart's scale. I settle on a simple triangular lathe outline for the cone so it stays solid and non-self-intersecting, and plan to paint a waffle-pattern texture onto it.

For the waffle, I define a paint function that alternates between two shades based on position to create a crosshatched lattice. I pick colors for the scoops—pink, mint, and chocolate—and then work out a generic dome outline helper using arc points from 0 to 90 degrees to build each rounded scoop shape as a lathe profile.

I lathe each scoop at its stacked height, then add a small sphere cherry on top. For the cart itself, I'm adding a rear handle bar made of rods, wheels, a possible tow bar, and small yellow sphere lights at the roof corners for decoration, plus considering polka-dot spotted paint for the mint-colored body.

For signage, I'm thinking of adding "ICE CREAM" lettering as a decal on both sides of the body, positioning it so the text faces outward correctly and mirroring it on the opposite side so it reads properly from each viewing angle.

Now I'm designing the sign texture with a cream background and bold red lettering, then moving to the awning stripes, counter tubs with tinted ice cream colors positioned along the counter top, and the front window frame dimensions.

With the window sitting below the counter overhang like a lit freezer display, I'm layering a cream border box behind a glass panel for depth. I'll skip adding a chalkboard menu for now and move on to setting up the base joint structure for the model's bones.

I'm settling on using a single root joint named "cart" with everything attaching to it by default, and planning the cylinder rotations for the wheels so their axis runs horizontally. For the paint patterns, I'm defining waffle-texture logic for the cone using height and angle values from the lathe surface, plus a palette of ice cream scoop colors like strawberry, mint, chocolate, and vanilla.

Now I'm working out the full vertical layout of the cart—body, roof, support posts, cone sign, stacked scoops, and cherry on top—calculating exact heights and radii so each piece nests naturally into the one below it, along with rod supports for the awning, handlebar, and roof posts, plus decals for the side and front signage and tub containers on the counter. I'm finalizing the body geometry with spot-paint coloring and striped awning paint, then writing the actual builder code to assemble all these parts together.

I'm now adding sprinkle decorations scattered across the scoop surfaces using randomized small capsule shapes in a few bright colors, filtered to the upper hemisphere of each scoop so they look naturally sprinkled on top. I'm also writing a dome-outline helper function for lathing the scoop shapes and finalizing the color palette constants for mint, cream, red, chrome, glass, and tire colors.

I'm now writing out the actual builder code—defining the paint patterns, constructing the body box, adding side and front decals, and building the menu board with support posts near the roof.
